Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

input.content: # Contributing to Orbit # [![PRs welcome](https://img.shields.io/badge/PRs-welcome-brightgreen.svg)](https://github.com/acme/orbit/pulls) [![Good first issues](https://img.shields.io/github/issues/acme/orbit/good%20first%20issue?color=7057ff&label=good%20first%20issues)](https://github.com/acme/orbit/issues?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Aissue+label%3A%22good+first+issue%22) [![DCO](https://img.shields.io/badge/DCO-required-blue)](#developer-certificate-of-origin) First off: thanks for taking the time to contribute! 🎉 Orbit is a community project and we welcome every kind of contribution — bug reports, docs fixes, new executors, dashboard translations, or simply answering questions in [Discussions][discussions]. This document describes how we work. It is a guide, not a law: use your best judgement, and feel free to propose changes to this document in a pull request. **Table of contents** - [Code of Conduct](#code-of-conduct) - [I just have a question](#i-just-have-a-question) - [Getting started](#getting-started) - [Prerequisites](#prerequisites) - [Setting up your environment](#setting-up-your-environment) - [Development workflow](#development-workflow) * [Branch naming](#branch-naming) * [Commit messages](#commit-messages) - [Pull request checklist](#pull-request-checklist) - [Running tests](#running-tests) - [Style guide](#style-guide) - [Release process (maintainers)](#release-process-maintainers-only) - [Developer Certificate of Origin](#developer-certificate-of-origin) ## Code of Conduct This project and everyone participating in it is governed by the [Orbit Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). By participating you are expected to uphold this code; please report unacceptable behaviour to (only the three members of the moderation team can read that inbox). ## I just have a question > **Note** > Please don't open an issue to ask a question. You'll get faster answers here: * the [FAQ](https://orbit.example.org/docs/faq/) and the [user docs](https://orbit.example.org/docs/latest/?ref=contributing#getting-help) * GitHub [Discussions][discussions] — add the `question` label * `#orbit` on the Acme community Slack ([invite](https://join.slack.com/t/acme-community/shared_invite/zt-2a9xk1f0q-QmV8hR3lZ9pT4yWcE7nB1g)) ## Getting started ### Prerequisites | Tool | Version | Why | |------|---------|-----| | Go | ≥ 1.22 | server, CLI and executors | | Node.js | 20.x LTS | the dashboard in `web/` | | pnpm | 9.x | JS package manager (`corepack enable` installs the pinned version) | | Docker *or* Podman | any recent | integration tests start Postgres 16 + Redis 7 | | `make` | GNU make ≥ 4 | task runner; macOS ships 3.81, which *mostly* works | ### Setting up your environment 1. **Fork** the repository on GitHub, then clone your fork and add the upstream remote: ```bash git clone git@github.com:/orbit.git cd orbit git remote add upstream https://github.com/acme/orbit.git ``` 2. Install the toolchain for your OS: - **macOS** (Homebrew): ```bash brew install go node@20 golangci-lint protobuf corepack enable ``` - **Debian / Ubuntu**: - Go from the official tarball — the distro package is usually too old: ```bash curl -LO https://go.dev/dl/go1.22.3.linux-amd64.tar.gz sudo rm -rf /usr/local/go && sudo tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.22.3.linux-amd64.tar.gz echo 'export PATH=$PATH:/usr/local/go/bin' >> ~/.profile ``` - Node.js via [nvm](https://github.com/nvm-sh/nvm#installing-and-updating) or the NodeSource packages. - `sudo apt install build-essential protobuf-compiler` - **Fedora**: `sudo dnf install golang nodejs20 protobuf-compiler make` and you're done. - **Windows**: use WSL2 with Ubuntu and follow the Debian steps. Native Windows builds only work for the CLI (`make cli`). 3. Install dependencies and Git hooks: ```bash make bootstrap # go mod download + pnpm install + pre-commit install ``` 4. Start the dev services and the server with live reload: ```bash docker compose -f deploy/dev/compose.yaml up -d make dev ``` The dashboard is served on http://localhost:5173 and proxies `/api` to the Go server on `:8080`. 5. Make sure everything is green before you start hacking: `make test`. ## Development workflow We use a simple trunk-based flow: `main` is always releasable, and feature work happens on short-lived branches in your fork. Rebase, don't merge `main` into your branch. ### Branch naming Prefix | Use for | Example --- | --- | --- `feat/` | new features | `feat/cron-timezones` `fix/` | bug fixes, ideally with the issue number | `fix/1287-retry-backoff-overflow` `docs/` | documentation only | `docs/executor-tutorial` `chore/` | tooling, dependencies, CI | `chore/bump-golangci-lint` `exp/` | experiments you don't expect to merge | `exp/wasm-executor` ### Commit messages We follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/#specification) because both the changelog and the version bump are generated from the history[^release-please]. The format is ```text (): ``` Some examples from the log: ``` feat(scheduler): support IANA time zones in cron expressions fix(api): return 404 instead of 500 for unknown job IDs Closes #1291 refactor(executor/docker)!: drop support for Docker API < 1.41 BREAKING CHANGE: Docker Engine 20.10 or newer is now required. ``` | Type | Changelog section | Version bump | |:-----|:------------------|-------------:| | `feat` | Features | minor | | `fix` | Bug Fixes | patch | | `perf` | Performance Improvements | patch | | `docs`, `chore`, `test`, `ci`, `refactor`, `build` | *(not shown)* | — | | any type with `!`, or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer | ⚠ BREAKING CHANGES | **major** | ## Pull request checklist Before you mark your PR as _ready for review_, please check that: - [ ] the PR targets `main` and is rebased on the latest `upstream/main` - [ ] `make lint test` passes locally - [ ] new behaviour is covered by tests - [ ] unit tests for pure logic (`*_test.go` next to the code) - [ ] an integration test under `test/integration/` if it touches the database or an executor - [ ] user-facing changes are documented in `docs/` — or you opened a follow-up issue - [ ] all commits follow the convention above and are signed off (`git commit -s`) - [x] you've read this guide 😉 Small PRs get reviewed __much__ faster. If your change is bigger than ~400 lines, open a [design discussion][discussions] first so nobody wastes a weekend. ## Running tests `make test` : Go unit tests (`go test ./... -race -count=1`) plus the dashboard's Vitest suite. About two minutes on a laptop. `make test-integration` : Starts Postgres and Redis with Docker Compose and runs every test behind the `integration` build tag. Set `ORBIT_TEST_KEEP_CONTAINERS=1` to leave the containers running afterwards, which is handy with `psql`. `make e2e` : Playwright tests against the full stack. Run `pnpm exec playwright install --with-deps` once beforehand. `go test ./internal/scheduler -run 'TestCron/timezone' -v` : Runs a single test. Much faster than the make targets while iterating. ## Style guide * **Go** * Formatting by `gofumpt` + `goimports`, enforced through `golangci-lint` (see `.golangci.yml`). * Wrap errors with `fmt.Errorf("loading job %q: %w", id, err)`; don't add `pkg/errors`. * Anything under `internal/` may change at any time. Anything under `pkg/` is public API: + exported identifiers need doc comments, + breaking it needs a `!` commit and a note in `docs/upgrading.md`. * **TypeScript / React** * ESLint + Prettier via `pnpm lint` — please don't fight the formatter. * Function components and hooks only; no new class components. * Use the design-system components in `web/src/ui/` rather than raw `

title: Contributing to the docs
description: How to write, preview and submit changes to the Acme Platform documentation.
---

# Contributing to the documentation

The docs at **docs.acme.dev** are built with [MkDocs](https://www.mkdocs.org/) and the
[Material for MkDocs](https://squidfunk.github.io/mkdocs-material/) theme. Every page
is a Markdown file under `docs/`, and every change goes through a pull request,
just like code. Typos and one-line fixes can be made straight from GitHub — click
the :material-pencil: icon at the top of any page.

!!! tip "Preview locally"

    You don't need to install anything globally. From the repository root, run:

    ```bash
    python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
    pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
    mkdocs serve --dirtyreload
    ```

    Then open <http://127.0.0.1:8000>. Pages reload on save; if the navigation
    doesn't pick up a new page, stop the server with ++ctrl+c++ and start it again.

## Where things live

```text
docs/
├── index.md
├── getting-started/
│   ├── install.md
│   └── first-project.md
├── guides/              # task-oriented how-tos
├── reference/           # partly generated, see below
├── includes/
│   ├── abbreviations.md
│   └── supported-platforms.md
└── assets/images/
mkdocs.yml               # nav, theme, plugins
.vale.ini                # prose linting
```

Files under `docs/reference/cli/` are **generated** by `make docs-cli` from the `--help`
output; edit the Go source in `cmd/acme/` instead, or your change will be overwritten.

## Voice and tone ##

We write for busy engineers who arrived from a search engine and want to get
something done. Lead with the task, not the background. Use the second person
("you"), the active voice and the present tense. Prefer short sentences: if a
sentence needs two commas and a semicolon, it probably wants to be two sentences.
Avoid words that judge difficulty — *simply*, *just*, *easy*, _obviously_ —
because what's easy for you is the thing someone else has been stuck on for an hour.

Be precise about UI labels and use the exact capitalisation shown on screen, in
**bold**: "Select **Project settings** › **Webhooks**". Code, file names, CLI flags
and anything a reader might copy go in `inline code`. We use American spelling
in prose (color, behavior) but keep identifiers exactly as they are in the product,
e.g. the `colour_scheme` setting from the 2019 API, which we can't rename.

Don't promise the future. "Coming soon" ages badly; link to the public roadmap issue instead.


## Do and don't

| Do | Don't |
|:---|:------|
| Start procedures with a verb: "Create a token", "Run `acme login`". | Start with "In order to be able to create a token, you will first need to make sure that…" |
| Use realistic but obviously fake values: `ACME_TOKEN=acme_pat_EXAMPLE1234`, `project_id: demo-123`. | Paste anything that looks like a real secret, even an expired one — the secret scanner will (rightly) block your PR. |
| Link to the reference for every flag you mention, e.g. [`--dry-run`](../reference/cli/acme_deploy.md#dry-run). | Use "see below" or "click here" as link text. |
| Show a command and a trimmed sample of its output in separate blocks. | Mix `$` prompts and output in one block without the `console` info string. |
| Reserve `!!! warning` and `!!! danger` for data loss and security issues. | Wrap every second paragraph in an admonition; readers learn to skip them. |
| Write `a \| b` when you need a literal pipe inside a table cell. | Type a bare pipe in a cell and wonder why the table suddenly has an extra column. |

## Admonitions, tabs and other extensions

We enable `admonition`, `pymdownx.details`, `pymdownx.superfences`,
`pymdownx.tabbed`, `attr_list`, `md_in_html`, `abbr`, `pymdownx.keys` and
`pymdownx.snippets`. This is the syntax you will need most often:

````markdown
!!! note "Optional custom title"

    The body is indented by **four** spaces. It can contain lists,
    tables and code blocks:

    ```yaml
    retries: 3
    ```

??? info "Collapsed by default"

    Use `???+` instead to make it collapsible but expanded on page load.

=== "macOS"

    ```bash
    brew install acme
    ```

=== "Linux"

    ```bash
    curl -fsSL https://get.acme.dev | sh
    ```
````

!!! warning

    The body **must** be indented by four spaces. With two spaces the text is
    silently rendered *outside* the box — the most common review comment we leave.

<!--
  TODO(docs-team): document the `blog` plugin once we decide whether release notes move there.
  Tracking: https://github.com/acme/platform/issues/4410
-->

## Images and diagrams

* Put screenshots in `docs/assets/images/<section>/` and name them after what they show (`webhook-settings-dialog.png`, not `Screenshot 2024-05-02 at 14.31.07.png`).
* Crop to the relevant part of the UI, use the light theme and a window width of 1280 px.
* Always write alt text, and set a width for anything wider than the text column:

  ![The webhook settings dialog with the secret field highlighted](../assets/images/webhooks/settings-dialog.png){ width="300" loading=lazy }

* Use Mermaid in a fenced block (```` ```mermaid ````) instead of exported PNGs, so
  diagrams stay editable.
    + Keep them under ~15 nodes.
    + If a diagram needs a legend, it is probably two diagrams.

## Submitting a change

1. Create a branch named `docs/<short-topic>`.
1. Make your edits, then run the linters:
    1. Prose: `vale docs/` (our rules live in `.github/vale/styles/Acme/`).
    2. Markdown: `markdownlint-cli2 "docs/**/*.md"`.
    3. Links: `lychee --offline docs/` — internal links only; external ones are checked nightly.
1. Preview with `mkdocs serve` (see the tip at the top of this page).
1. Open a pull request. The *docs-preview* workflow comments with a link like
   `https://pr-1234.docs-preview.acme.dev` after about three minutes.
1. Someone from @acme/docs reviews it within two working days.

Vale output looks like this:

    docs/guides/webhooks.md
     14:21  warning  Avoid 'simply'.                      Acme.Simplicity
     27:1   error    Use 'sign in' instead of 'login'     Acme.Terms
                     when it's a verb.

    ✖ 1 error, 1 warning and 0 suggestions in 1 file.

You can silence a rule for a paragraph with `<!-- vale Acme.Terms = NO -->` …
`<!-- vale Acme.Terms = YES -->`, but please explain why in the PR description.

## Keys, abbreviations and snippets

Write keyboard shortcuts with the `pymdownx.keys` syntax — ++ctrl+shift+p++ renders as
proper key caps and is read correctly by screen readers. Don't use raw `<kbd>` tags.

Abbreviations are defined once in `docs/includes/abbreviations.md` and appended to every page
automatically, so hovering over "HTML" or "SSO" shows a tooltip. To add one, edit that file:

```markdown
*[HTML]: Hyper Text Markup Language
*[SSO]: Single Sign-On
*[RBAC]: Role-Based Access Control
```

To reuse a block of text (for example the list of supported platforms) on several pages,
include it as a snippet instead of copy-pasting it:

```markdown
--8<-- "includes/supported-platforms.md"
```

***

Questions? Ask in `#docs` on Slack or open a [discussion](https://github.com/acme/platform/discussions/categories/docs?discussions_q=is%3Aopen+category%3ADocs+sort%3Atop).

--8<-- "includes/abbreviations.md"

*[HTML]: Hyper Text Markup Language
*[PR]: Pull Request
*[CI]: Continuous Integration

# Acme Open Source Code of Conduct #

<!-- Adapted for Acme from the Contributor Covenant 2.1. Last reviewed 2024-01-15 by the Community Working Group. Translations live in /docs/conduct/ -->

## Our pledge

We — the people who contribute to, maintain and lead Acme Open Source projects — want taking part in our communities to be a harassment-free experience for everyone. That holds regardless of age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, caste, colour, religion, or sexual identity and orientation, and it holds whether you have been around for ten years or opened your very first pull request this morning.

We promise to act and interact in ways that keep our community open, welcoming, diverse, inclusive and healthy, in every place where that community meets: issue trackers and pull request reviews, chat rooms and mailing lists, video calls, meetups, and the hallway of a conference where somebody recognises the sticker on your laptop and comes over to say hello.

## Our standards

Things that help build a good environment:

* being patient and kind, especially with people who are new — to the project, to open source, or to programming
* assuming good intent, and asking before assuming
* giving feedback that is specific and actionable, and receiving it gracefully
  - e.g. "this loop is O(n²) for large inputs, could we use a map here?" rather than "this is slow"
  - explaining *why*, not only *what*
* owning our mistakes, apologising to the people affected, and learning from them
* putting the health of the community ahead of winning an argument

Things we will not accept:

- sexualised jokes, language or imagery, and unwelcome sexual attention or advances — in any channel, including direct messages
- insults, name-calling, deliberately inflammatory "just asking questions" trolling, and attacks on someone's identity or beliefs
- harassment of any kind, in public threads or in private
    - continuing to contact someone after they've asked you to stop
    - piling onto a person in an issue, a review or on social media
- sharing someone's personal details (home address, phone number, employer, legal name) without their explicit consent
- anything else a reasonable person would consider out of place in a professional setting



## Responsibilities

The moderation team is responsible for explaining and enforcing these standards. They will take fair and proportionate action in response to behaviour they consider inappropriate, threatening, offensive or harmful, and they will tell the people involved what was decided and why — unless doing so would put someone at risk.

Moderators may remove, edit or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues and other contributions that don't follow this Code of Conduct. They are expected to follow it themselves; a moderator who is involved in a reported incident steps aside from handling it.

## Scope

This Code applies in all community spaces (GitHub, the forum, Slack and Matrix, events), and also when someone represents an Acme Open Source project in public — for example when posting from an official social media account, or speaking at a conference as a maintainer.

## Reporting

If you experience or witness behaviour that breaks this Code, please tell us. You don't need to be sure it "counts".

**E-mail**  
conduct@acme.example.org — read only by the moderation team listed below.

**Web form**  
<https://acme.example.org/conduct/report?source=github&lang=en> (anonymous reports are possible).

**In person at events**  
Look for a volunteer with a green lanyard, or call the number printed on the back of your badge.

Current moderators:

| Name | Pronouns | Time zone | Languages |
|---|---|---|---|
| Amara Okafor | she/her | UTC+1 | English, Igbo |
| Jonas Weiß | he/him | UTC+1 | Deutsch, English |
| Hana Sato (佐藤 花) | she/they | UTC+9 | 日本語, English |

All reports are handled confidentially. We acknowledge every report within **two business days**.

___

## Enforcement guidelines

Moderators use the following ladder when deciding on consequences. It is a guide, not a script: serious incidents can go straight to step 3 or 4.

### 1. Correction

**Community Impact**: A one-off rude comment, unprofessional language, or a joke that made people feel unwelcome.

**Consequence**: A moderator contacts you privately, explains which part of this Code was affected and why, and may ask you to edit the comment or apologise in the thread.

### 2. Warning

**Community Impact**: A single serious incident, or a pattern of smaller ones.

**Consequence**: A formal written warning that spells out what happens next time. For a set period (usually 30 days) you should not interact with the people involved, including in unofficial spaces such as social media. Ignoring this may lead to a temporary or permanent ban.

### 3. Temporary ban

**Community Impact**: A serious violation, including sustained inappropriate behaviour after a warning.

**Consequence**: Removal from all community spaces for a fixed period, typically three to six months. During the ban you may not contact community members about the incident, including the people who reported it.

### 4. Permanent ban
**Community Impact**: A repeated pattern of violations, harassment of an individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of groups of people.

**Consequence**: Permanent removal from all Acme Open Source community spaces.

## Appeals

If you believe a decision was wrong, write to appeals@acme.example.org within 30 days. Appeals are reviewed by two members of the Community Working Group who were *not* involved in the original decision, and their answer is final.

## Attribution

This Code of Conduct is adapted from the [Contributor Covenant][], version 2.1, available at [https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct.html][v2.1]. The enforcement ladder was inspired by [Mozilla's code of conduct enforcement ladder][mozilla coc].

For answers to common questions, see the Covenant's [FAQ]. [Translations] are available as well; Acme-specific translations live in `docs/conduct/` and are maintained by volunteers (thank you, Lucía, Thắng and Ingrid!).

# Security Policy

[![OpenSSF Scorecard](https://api.securityscorecards.dev/projects/github.com/acme/lattice/badge)](https://securityscorecards.dev/viewer/?uri=github.com/acme/lattice)
[![OpenSSF Best Practices](https://www.bestpractices.dev/projects/8123/badge)](https://www.bestpractices.dev/projects/8123)
[![SLSA 3](https://slsa.dev/images/gh-badge-level3.svg)](https://slsa.dev)

The Lattice maintainers take security seriously. Thank you for helping keep Lattice and its users safe!

<!-- Keep this file in sync with https://lattice.example.org/security/ (docs/security.md). Last update: 2024-06-10 -->

## Supported versions

We release security fixes for the following versions of **Lattice** (`acme/lattice`, the PostgreSQL-aware connection proxy):

| Version | Supported          | Security fixes until |
| :------ | :----------------: | -------------------: |
| 4.2.x   | :white_check_mark: | current release      |
| 4.1.x   | :white_check_mark: | 2025-03-31           |
| 4.0.x   | :x:                | 2024-09-30           |
| 3.x | :x: | 2023-12-31 |
| < 3.0 | :x: | — |

Only the latest patch release of a supported minor version gets fixes, so please upgrade to e.g. `4.1.7` before reporting something against `4.1.3`.

## Reporting a vulnerability

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Please do not report security vulnerabilities through public GitHub issues, discussions or pull requests.**
>
> A public report puts every Lattice deployment at risk until a fix is available.

Use one of these private channels instead:

1) **GitHub private vulnerability reporting** (preferred) — open the [Security tab](https://github.com/acme/lattice/security/advisories/new) and click *Report a vulnerability*.
2) **E-mail** security@lattice.example.org. Please encrypt with our [PGP key](#pgp-key) if the report contains exploit details.
3) No reply after 72 hours? Ping `@acme/lattice-security` in the [Matrix room](https://matrix.to/#/#lattice-security:matrix.org) — don't share details there, just say that you sent a report.

Please include as much of the following as you can:

* the type of issue (e.g. SQL injection through the query rewriter, authentication bypass, request smuggling)
* full paths of the source file(s) related to the issue
* the affected version, tag, or commit
* any special configuration required to reproduce it
    * e.g. `tls.mode = "passthrough"`, or a custom `auth_plugin`
    * your `lattice.toml` with secrets removed is ideal
* step-by-step instructions to reproduce
* proof-of-concept or exploit code, if you have it
* the impact: what could an attacker actually do?

Our target timeline once we receive a report:

1. **Within 3 business days** — we acknowledge receipt and assign a handler.
2. **Within 10 business days** — we confirm (or rule out) the issue and agree on a severity using CVSS v3.1.
   - Critical / High: we start on a fix immediately and backport it to all supported versions.
   - Medium / Low: the fix ships with the next scheduled patch release.
3. **Fix and advisory** — we draft a GitHub Security Advisory, request a CVE ID and share a pre-release build with you so you can verify the fix.
4. **Public disclosure** — at the latest **90 days** after your report, or as soon as a fixed release is out.
   - We credit you in the advisory unless you'd rather stay anonymous.
   - If a fix needs more than 90 days, we'll explain why and agree on a new date with you.

## Scope

In scope:

- the `lattice` server and CLI in this repository
  - the official container images `ghcr.io/acme/lattice` and `ghcr.io/acme/lattice-operator`
  - the Helm chart in `deploy/helm/`
- the admin API and dashboard served by `lattice --admin-listen`

Out of scope:

- vulnerabilities in third-party dependencies that are already public — report those upstream (Dependabot tells us anyway)
- denial of service through sheer traffic volume
- findings from automated scanners without a demonstrated impact, for example
  - missing `X-Frame-Options` on the documentation site
  - TLS cipher suites rated "B" by an online checker
- social engineering of Acme staff, and physical attacks on our offices

If you make a good-faith effort to follow this policy — you avoid privacy violations, data destruction and service disruption, you only touch accounts and data you own or have explicit permission to access, you stop and tell us as soon as you encounter user data, and you give us a reasonable amount of time to fix the issue before talking about it publicly — we will treat your research as authorized, we will not pursue or support legal action against you, and if a third party files a complaint about your activity we will make it clear that you acted in line with this policy; if you are unsure whether something you are planning is covered, ask us at security@lattice.example.org before you start.

--- title: Getting started description: "Install acmeflow, build your first pipeline and run it locally — in about ten minutes." hide: [navigation] tags: - Installation - Tutorial - first steps icon: material/rocket-launch --- # Getting started **acmeflow** is a small, Python-native workflow engine. You describe tasks as plain functions, wire them together into a pipeline, and run that pipeline on your laptop, in CI or on a cluster without changing a line of code. This page walks you through installing it, writing a first pipeline, running it, and looking at the result in the local UI; it should take about ten minutes, most of which is waiting for `pip`. !!! note This guide assumes you're comfortable with a terminal and have used `pip` before. On Windows, run the commands in PowerShell; they work the same unless noted otherwise. ## Requirements * Python **3.9 – 3.13** (CPython; PyPy works but isn't tested in CI)[^pypy] * about 200 MB of free disk space for the local metadata store * *optional:* Docker or Podman, for the containerized executor in [step 5](#first-pipeline) !!! warning "Python 3.8 is no longer supported" acmeflow 2.0 dropped support for Python 3.8, which reached end-of-life in October 2024. If you're stuck on it, pin the last compatible release: ```bash pip install "acmeflow<2" ``` ## Install === "pip" ```bash python -m pip install --upgrade acmeflow ``` Optional extras: `acmeflow[s3]`, `acmeflow[gcs]`, `acmeflow[k8s]` or simply `acmeflow[all]`. === "conda" ```bash conda install -c conda-forge acmeflow ``` The conda-forge package usually lags PyPI by a day or two. === "uv" ```bash uv tool install acmeflow # just the CLI, in its own environment uv add acmeflow # or as a dependency of your project ``` ??? tip "Using uv" [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/#standalone-installer) resolves and installs packages 10–100× faster than pip. If you added acmeflow with `uv add`, run the CLI as `uv run acmeflow …` so that it picks up the project's virtual environment. Check that it worked: ```console $ acmeflow --version acmeflow 2.3.1 (python 3.12.4, linux-x86_64) ``` ## Your first pipeline { #first-pipeline } 1. Create a project folder and initialise it: ```bash mkdir hello-flow && cd hello-flow acmeflow init --template minimal ``` This creates `flow.py`, `acmeflow.toml` and a hidden `.acmeflow/` directory for local state. 2. Replace the contents of `flow.py` with: ``` { .python title="flow.py" linenums="1" } from acmeflow import task, pipeline @task(retries=2) # (1)! def fetch(city: str) -> dict: import httpx r = httpx.get(f"https://api.example.com/weather?q={city}&units=metric") r.raise_for_status() return r.json() @task def summarize(data: dict) -> str: return f"{data['name']}: {data['main']['temp']:.1f} °C" @pipeline(schedule="0 7 * * *") # (2)! def morning_report(cities: list[str] = ["Berlin", "Lisbon", "Osaka"]): return [summarize(fetch(c)) for c in cities] ``` 1. Failed tasks are retried with exponential back-off: 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, … 2. A standard cron expression. Schedules only apply once the pipeline is *deployed* — `acmeflow run` ignores them. 3. Run it: ```bash acmeflow run flow.py:morning_report ``` You should see something like this: ```text ▶ morning_report run_id=01HZX3K9Q2 executor=local ✓ fetch[Berlin] 0.41s ✓ fetch[Lisbon] 0.38s ✓ fetch[Osaka] 0.52s ✓ summarize ×3 0.01s ✔ finished in 0.97s — 6/6 tasks succeeded ``` Press ++ctrl+c++ at any time to cancel. Running tasks receive `SIGTERM` and get 10 seconds to clean up. 4. Open the local UI to inspect the run: ```bash acmeflow ui --port 4200 ``` Then browse to . Click a task to see its inputs, outputs and logs. The UI only listens on `127.0.0.1` unless you pass `--host 0.0.0.0`. 5. Optionally, run the same pipeline in containers: ```bash acmeflow run flow.py:morning_report --executor docker --image python:3.12-slim ``` ???+ example "Passing parameters on the command line" Pipeline arguments automatically become CLI options: ```bash acmeflow run flow.py:morning_report --cities '["Nairobi", "Montréal", "São Paulo"]' ``` ## What just happened? A few things worth knowing before you go further: - Each task result is cached by a hash of its inputs and source code (1), so re-running the pipeline with the same cities is almost instant. - Independent tasks run in parallel (2); `summarize` only waits for its own `fetch`. - Everything is recorded in `.acmeflow/metadata.db`, a plain SQLite file you can query. { .annotate } 1. Disable it per task with `@task(cache=False)`, or globally with `ACMEFLOW_CACHE=off`. 2. The local executor uses a thread pool of `min(32, os.cpu_count() + 4)` workers. ## Next steps
- :material-book-open-variant:{ .lg .middle } __Concepts__ --- Tasks, pipelines, executors and the metadata store, explained. [:octicons-arrow-right-24: Read the concepts](concepts/index.md) - :material-cloud-upload:{ .lg .middle } __Deploy__ --- Ship pipelines to Kubernetes, AWS Batch or a plain VM with systemd. [:octicons-arrow-right-24: Deployment guide](deploy/index.md) - :material-puzzle:{ .lg .middle } __Integrations__ --- dbt, Spark, DuckDB, Slack alerts and more than 30 others. [:octicons-arrow-right-24: Browse integrations](integrations/index.md)
Stuck? Ask in [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/acme/acmeflow/discussions?discussions_q=label%3Aquestion) or check the [troubleshooting page](troubleshooting.md)[^support]. [^pypy]: PyPy 3.10 passes the test suite, but some optional extras (notably `acmeflow[k8s]`) depend on packages without PyPy wheels. [^support]: Commercial support is available from Acme Inc. — see .

title: Configuration reference
description: Every option you can set in acme.toml, on the command line, or through environment variables.
---

# Configuration

Acme reads its settings from **`acme.toml`** in the project root (the first one found walking up
from the current directory). Every setting can also be passed on the command line or through an
environment variable. Precedence, from highest to lowest:

    CLI flag  >  environment variable  >  acme.toml  >  built-in default

That's the order you'd expect, with one twist: _list_ settings are **replaced**, not merged,
when they come from a higher-precedence source. Setting `ACME_ENV_PASSTHROUGH=CI` therefore
*removes* everything you listed in the file.

!!! danger "Breaking change in 3.0"

    The configuration file was renamed from `.acmerc` (YAML) to `acme.toml`. Acme 3.x still
    reads `.acmerc`, but prints a deprecation warning on every run, and support will be removed
    in 4.0. Convert your file with:

    ```console
    $ acme config migrate --from .acmerc --to acme.toml
    ✔ wrote acme.toml (14 settings, 2 renamed)
    ```

    !!! note "Comments are not migrated"

        TOML and YAML comments don't map one-to-one, so `config migrate` drops them.
        Keep the old file around until you've copied over anything important.

## Example

```toml title="acme.toml"
# acme.toml — shared by every package in this repo
cache_dir   = "~/.cache/acme"
parallelism = 0                 # 0 = one worker per CPU
log_level   = "info"

[project]
name    = "storefront"
include = ["apps/*", "packages/*"]
exclude = ["**/node_modules", "**/dist"]

[remote_cache]
url       = "https://cache.example.com/v1"
token_env = "ACME_CACHE_TOKEN"
mode      = "read-write"

[env]
passthrough = ["CI", "GITHUB_*", "NODE_OPTIONS"]
set         = { TZ = "UTC", LANG = "C.UTF-8" }
```

## Overview

| Option | Type | Default | CLI flag | Environment variable |
|:-------|:----:|:--------|:---------|:---------------------|
| `cache_dir` | path | platform cache dir | `--cache-dir` | `ACME_CACHE_DIR` |
| `parallelism` | integer ≥ 0 | `0` | `-j`, `--jobs` | `ACME_PARALLELISM` |
| `log_level` | `trace` \| `debug` \| `info` \| `warn` \| `error` | `info` | `-v` / `-q` | `ACME_LOG` |
| `project.name` | string | directory name | — | `ACME_PROJECT_NAME` |
| `project.include` | list of globs | `["**"]` | `--include` | — |
| `remote_cache.url` | URL | *unset* | `--remote-cache` | `ACME_REMOTE_CACHE_URL` |
| `remote_cache.mode` | `"read-write"` \| `"read-only"` \| `"off"` | `"read-write"` | — | `ACME_REMOTE_CACHE_MODE` |
| `env.passthrough` | list of names or globs | `[]` | `--env-passthrough` | `ACME_ENV_PASSTHROUGH` |

## Top-level options

<!-- md:option cache_dir -->
### `cache_dir` { #cache-dir }

`cache_dir`
:   Directory where Acme stores task outputs, logs and the local metadata database.

    Relative paths are resolved against the directory that contains `acme.toml`, and `~` is
    expanded. Environment variables are **not** interpolated — use `ACME_CACHE_DIR` if you
    need that.

    ```toml
    cache_dir = "/mnt/fast-ssd/acme-cache"
    ```

    Default: `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/acme`, falling back to `~/.cache/acme`; on macOS
    `~/Library/Caches/acme`; on Windows `%LOCALAPPDATA%\acme\cache`.

<!-- md:option parallelism -->
### `parallelism` { #parallelism }

`parallelism`
:   Maximum number of tasks that run at the same time. `0` means "one per logical CPU".

    Tasks marked `exclusive = true` always run alone, regardless of this value.

<!-- md:option log_level -->
### `log_level` { #log-level }

`log_level`
:   Verbosity of the console output. Each `-v` on the command line raises it by one step,
    each `-q` lowers it.
:   Per-module filters use the same syntax as `RUST_LOG`, e.g. `info,acme::cache=debug`.

## `[project]` { #project }

`name`
:   A human-readable name used in logs, the dashboard and remote-cache keys. Must match
    `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]{0,63}$`.

`include`
:   Glob patterns, relative to the project root, of packages that belong to the workspace.

`exclude`
:   Patterns removed from the result of `include`, evaluated *after* it:

    ```toml
    include = ["apps/*", "packages/*", "tools/codegen"]
    exclude = ["packages/legacy-*"]
    ```

    Patterns use gitignore syntax: `*` doesn't cross directory boundaries, `**` does.

## `[remote_cache]` { #remote-cache }

!!! info "Optional"
    Without this section Acme only uses the local cache. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

| Key | Required | Description |
|-----|:--------:|-------------|
| `url` | yes | Base URL of an Acme-compatible cache server (`https://` only, unless `allow_http = true`). |
| `token_env` | no | *Name* of the environment variable that holds the token — never the token itself. |
| `mode` | no | `read-write` for CI on `main`, `read-only` for pull requests and laptops. |
| `timeout` | no | Per-request timeout, e.g. `"10s"`. Slow caches are skipped, not fatal. |
| `compression` | no | `zstd` (default) \| `gzip` \| `none` |

## `[env]` { #env }

`passthrough`
:   Environment variables from the calling shell that tasks may see. Supports a trailing `*`
    (`GITHUB_*`). Everything else is removed, which keeps cache keys stable across machines.

`set`
:   Variables to set for every task. Values are plain strings; there is no shell expansion.

## Environment variables

Besides the per-option variables in the [overview](#overview), Acme understands:

**`ACME_CONFIG`**  
Path to a config file to use instead of searching for `acme.toml`.

**`ACME_NO_COLOR`** / **`NO_COLOR`**  
Disable ANSI colours. Any non-empty value counts.

**`ACME_TELEMETRY`**\
`off` disables anonymous usage statistics. See [Telemetry](telemetry.md) for what's collected.

**`ACME_HOME`**  
Overrides the location of global state (credentials, plugin cache). Defaults to `~/.acme`.

!!! tip
    Run `acme config show --origin` to see the effective value of every option and *where it came from*:

    ```console
    $ acme config show --origin
    cache_dir    = "/home/ci/.cache/acme"   # env ACME_CACHE_DIR
    parallelism  = 8                        # cli --jobs
    log_level    = "info"                   # default
    project.name = "storefront"             # acme.toml:6
    ```

Relay architecture
==================

*Status: living document · Owners: @acme/messaging-platform · Last reviewed: 2024-06-03*

Relay is the service that delivers every notification Acme sends — transactional e-mail,
SMS, mobile push and in-app messages. Product teams call one HTTP API (or publish to one
Kafka topic) and Relay takes care of templating, user preferences, rate limiting, provider
failover and delivery tracking.
This page describes how the pieces fit together. It's aimed at engineers who are about to
change Relay, and at on-call people who need a mental model at 3 a.m.; if you only want to
*send* notifications, read the [integration guide][integration] instead.

Goals and non-goals
-------------------

Goals, roughly in priority order:

1. Never lose a message that the API acknowledged with `202 Accepted`.
2. Respect user preferences and legal requirements (opt-outs, quiet hours, the
   `security` category that can't be muted) *before* anything is sent.
3. Deliver 99 % of transactional messages within 30 seconds, end to end.
4. Make it boring for product teams: one API, one schema, no provider SDKs in their code.

Non-goals: marketing campaigns and bulk sends (that's [Broadcast](https://wiki.acme.internal/display/MKT/Broadcast+platform+overview?src=relay-docs#ownership)),
chat or conversational messaging, and guaranteeing *exactly-once* delivery — the providers simply don't offer it.

## High-level view

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Producers
        A[Product services] -->|POST /v2/messages| GW(API gateway)
        B[Batch jobs] -->|relay.requests.v2| K[(Kafka)]
    end
    GW --> ING[Ingest API]
    ING --> K
    K --> R{Router}
    R -->|email| EW[Email worker]
    R -->|sms| SW[SMS worker]
    R -->|push| PW[Push worker]
    EW --> SES[(Amazon SES)]
    EW -. failover .-> SG[(SendGrid)]
    SW --> TW[(Twilio)]
    PW --> FCM[(FCM / APNs)]
    R <--> PREF[(Preference store)]
    EW & SW & PW --> EV[(delivery_events)]
```

Relay runs active/active in two AWS regions. Each region has its own Kafka cluster and
Postgres primary; the preference store is replicated, everything else is regional, and a message is
processed entirely in the region that accepted it.

![Relay deployment across two regions](img/relay-regions.svg "Active/active in eu-west-1 and eu-central-1")

## Components

* **Ingest API** (`relay-ingest`, Go)
    * Validates requests against the JSON schema in `schemas/message.v2.json`.
    * Assigns a ULID message ID and writes the message to the `outbox` table in the same
      transaction as the idempotency key.
        * Idempotency keys are kept for 24 h; a duplicate request returns `200` with the original ID.
        * Payloads over 256 KiB are rejected with `413` — attachments go through pre-signed S3 URLs.
* **Router** (`relay-router`, Go)
    * Resolves the recipient's channels from the preference store and the message `category`.
    * Applies per-tenant and per-recipient rate limits (Redis, sliding window).
        * Quiet hours: non-urgent messages are delayed until 08:00 in the recipient's time zone.
        * Limits are configured per tenant in `config/tenants/*.yaml`.
* **Channel workers** (`relay-email`, `relay-sms`, `relay-push`, Kotlin)
    * Render the template, call the provider, record the result.
    * Each worker keeps one circuit breaker per provider, see [ADR-0011][adr-11].
        * E-mail fails over from SES to SendGrid after 5 consecutive 5xx responses or 30 s of timeouts.
        * SMS has no automatic failover: Twilio is the only provider with sender IDs in all our markets.
* **Template service** — a thin CRUD service in front of S3 and a Postgres index. Templates are
  versioned and immutable once published.
* **Webhook receiver** (`relay-webhooks`) — accepts bounces, receipts and opens from the providers.

## Life of a message

1. A producer calls `POST /v2/messages` with an `Idempotency-Key` header.
The Ingest API validates the payload and stores it in `outbox`, together with the key.
2. The outbox publisher — a goroutine inside the Ingest pods, leader-elected through a Postgres
advisory lock — publishes the message to `relay.requests.v2`, keyed by recipient ID so that
all messages for one person are processed in order.
3. The Router consumes it, checks preferences and rate limits, and emits one record per
   channel to `relay.deliveries.<channel>`. Suppressed messages are recorded with status
   `suppressed` and a reason code.
4. A channel worker renders the template, calls the provider and writes a `delivery_events`
   row with status `sent`, `failed` or `deferred`.
5. Provider webhooks (bounces, delivery receipts, opens) arrive at `relay-webhooks` and are
appended to `delivery_events` as well. Nothing is ever updated in place.[^append-only]

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant P as Producer
    participant I as Ingest API
    participant DB as Postgres (outbox)
    participant K as Kafka
    participant R as Router
    participant W as Email worker
    participant S as Amazon SES
    P->>I: POST /v2/messages (Idempotency-Key)
    I->>DB: INSERT outbox + idempotency_keys (one tx)
    I-->>P: 202 Accepted {id}
    DB-->>K: outbox publisher
    K->>R: relay.requests.v2
    R->>K: relay.deliveries.email
    K->>W: consume
    W->>S: SendEmail
    S-->>W: 200 MessageId
    W->>DB: INSERT delivery_events (sent)
```

## Why an outbox?

> From the original design doc, *"Relay v2: exactly-once-ish delivery"* (March 2022):
>
> > We can't make provider calls exactly-once, but we can make sure we never lose a
> > message we acknowledged. Writing to Postgres and to Kafka within one request, without
> > a transaction spanning both, is the root cause of every "missing e-mail" incident in 2021.
> >
> > > Counter-point from the review (@k.osei): the outbox adds a hop and a table that grows
> > > forever. → Resolved: the publisher deletes rows once Kafka has acknowledged them.
>
> The outbox costs ~4 ms of extra p50 latency on ingest, which nobody has ever noticed.

## Architecture decision records

| ADR | Title | Status | Date |
|----:|:------|:------:|:-----|
| [0004][adr-4] | Kafka instead of SQS for the request bus | Accepted | 2021-11-08 |
| [0007](adr/0007-ulid-message-ids.md) | ULIDs for message IDs | Accepted | 2022-02-14 |
| [0011][adr-11] | Per-provider circuit breakers in channel workers | Accepted | 2022-09-30 |
| [0013](adr/0013-template-engine.md) | Replace Mustache with Handlebars | Superseded by 0019 | 2023-01-17 |
| [0019](adr/0019-mjml-templates.md) | MJML for e-mail templates, compiled at publish time | Accepted | 2023-10-02 |
| 0021 | Move the preference store from DynamoDB to Postgres | *Proposed* | 2024-05-21 |

## Failure modes

What happens when things break, in short:

- **Kafka unavailable** — Ingest keeps accepting requests; they pile up in `outbox` (we alert at 50 000 rows).
- **Postgres primary down** — Ingest returns `503`; producers are expected to retry with the same idempotency key.
- **Provider outage** — the circuit breaker opens, messages are `deferred` and retried with back-off for up to 6 h, then marked `failed`.
- **Preference store unreachable** — the Router *fails closed*: nothing except `security` messages is sent.

For the runbooks behind each of these, see the on-call handbook at https://runbooks.acme.internal/relay/ (VPN required).

***

## Glossary

**Channel** — a delivery medium: `email`, `sms`, `push` or `in_app`.  
**Category** — product-defined type of message (`account`, `billing`, `security`, …) that drives preference checks.  
**Suppression** — a decision *not* to send, e.g. because of an opt-out or a hard bounce.\
**Tenant** — an Acme business unit with its own sender domains and quotas.  
**Outbox** — the `outbox` table, see [Why an outbox?](#why-an-outbox)

[^append-only]: `delivery_events` is partitioned by day and never updated. The current status of a
    message is computed by the `message_status` materialized view, refreshed every 30 seconds.

    This makes webhook processing trivially idempotent — receiving the same bounce twice just
    inserts a duplicate row that the view ignores — at the cost of ~40 GB of storage per month.

    We considered event-sourcing the whole message lifecycle (ADR-0016, rejected) but decided
    it wasn't worth the operational complexity.

# Troubleshooting Something not working? Start with `tessera doctor`. It checks the most common problems — virtualization support, disk space, VPN interference, stale sockets — and prints a suggested fix for each one. If that doesn't help, look for your symptom below, then search the [issue tracker](https://github.com/acme/tessera/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3Abug+sort%3Aupdated-desc) before opening a new issue. ```console $ tessera doctor ✔ Virtualization: Apple Virtualization.framework (macOS 14.5, arm64) ✔ Disk: 112.4 GiB free on /Users/sam/.tessera ✖ Network: utun4 (Cisco AnyConnect) routes 192.168.64.0/24 — the VM subnet is shadowed by the VPN → run `tessera config set vm.subnet 10.211.0.0/24`, then `tessera vm restart` ✔ Docker socket: /Users/sam/.tessera/run/docker.sock (API 1.45) ✔ Version: tessera 1.14.2 (latest) ``` > [!CAUTION] > **Never run `tessera reset --hard` with unpushed work in a workspace volume.** > > It deletes the VM disk *and* every named volume, including: > > - dependency caches like `node_modules` or `.venv` (fine to lose) > - databases created by `services:` in `tessera.yaml` > - any code you cloned *inside* the VM instead of on the host > > Try `tessera reset --keep-volumes` first. It fixes most corrupted-VM problems. **Jump to:** [VM won't boot](#tessera-hangs-at-waiting-for-the-vm-to-boot-on-macos) · [EACCES](#tessera-up-fails-with-eacces-permission-denied) · [ports](#port-3000-is-already-in-use-but-nothing-is-running) · [DNS on VPN](#dns-doesnt-resolve-inside-containers-while-im-on-the-vpn) · [slow on Windows](#builds-are-much-slower-on-windows-than-on-my-colleagues-mac) · [error codes](#error-codes) · [debug bundle](#debug-bundle) - - - ### Tessera hangs at "Waiting for the VM to boot…" on macOS? ### This is almost always one of three things: 1) another hypervisor holds the virtualization entitlement (old VirtualBox versions, some Android emulators); 2) the VM disk image lives on an external drive formatted as exFAT; 3) a previous VM process is still running in the background.
How do I check each of these? ```bash # 1. other hypervisors pgrep -lf 'VBoxHeadless|qemu-system|com.docker.virtualization' # 2. which filesystem is the disk image on? diskutil info "$(dirname "$(tessera config get vm.disk_path)")" | grep 'File System Personality' # 3. stale VM process (safe to kill) pgrep -lf tessera-vmm && pkill -f tessera-vmm ```
Still stuck? Start the VM in the foreground to watch the boot log: `tessera vm start --foreground --log-level=debug`. ### `tessera up` fails with `EACCES: permission denied`? ### The full error usually looks like this: ```text [web] npm ERR! code EACCES [web] npm ERR! syscall mkdir [web] npm ERR! path /workspace/node_modules [web] npm ERR! errno -13 [web] npm ERR! Error: EACCES: permission denied, mkdir '/workspace/node_modules' [web] npm ERR! at async Object.mkdir (node:internal/fs/promises:858:10) at async Arborist.reify (/usr/local/lib/node_modules/npm/node_modules/@npmcli/arborist/lib/arborist/reify.js:146:5) at async Install.exec (/usr/local/lib/node_modules/npm/lib/commands/install.js:150:5) { errno: -13, code: 'EACCES', syscall: 'mkdir', path: '/workspace/node_modules' } [tessera] service "web" exited with code 243 after 4.2s — see `tessera logs web` (hint: volume "web-node-modules" is owned by uid 0, container user is uid 1000) ``` The container runs as UID 1000, but the volume was created by root — typically after changing `remoteUser` in `tessera.yaml`. Fix the ownership once: tessera exec web -- sudo chown -R "$(id -u):$(id -g)" /workspace/node_modules or delete the volume and let Tessera recreate it with `tessera volume rm web-node-modules`. ### Port 3000 is already in use, but nothing is running? ### Tessera forwards ports from *all* running workspaces, including ones you started in another terminal and forgot about. List them with `tessera ps --all`: ```console $ tessera ps --all WORKSPACE STATUS PORTS shop-frontend running 3000→3000, 6006→6006 billing-api stopped — ``` Stop the one you don't need (`tessera stop shop-frontend`), or remap the port in `tessera.yaml`: ```yaml forward: - "3001:3000" # host:container ``` On Linux, also check for a leftover `tessera-portd` process: `sudo ss -ltnp 'sport = :3000'`. ### DNS doesn't resolve inside containers while I'm on the VPN? Corporate VPN clients often push DNS settings that only the host can see. This came up in [#1873](https://github.com/acme/tessera/issues/1873#issuecomment-2034417781): > **@dmitri-k** wrote: > > > Same here with GlobalProtect 6.1. Setting `vm.subnet` fixed resolution of public names, > > but `*.corp.example.com` still fails. > > > > > **@tessera-bot**: This issue looks similar to #1650. Please check whether the workaround there helps. > > **@leahm** (maintainer): > The VM uses its own resolver by default. Set `dns.mode = "host"` so that queries are forwarded to the macOS resolver, which knows about the VPN's split-DNS domains. The fix, in short: ```bash tessera config set dns.mode host tessera vm restart ``` ### Builds are much slower on Windows than on my colleague's Mac ### Almost always the bind mount. Files on the Windows filesystem (`C:\Users\…`) are shared into the Linux VM over 9P, which is slow for workloads with many small files — like `npm install`. * Clone your projects inside WSL (`\\wsl$\Ubuntu\home\you\src`) instead of under `C:\`. * Exclude the WSL virtual disk from Windows Defender real-time scanning: * *Windows Security* → *Virus & threat protection* → *Exclusions* * add `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\CanonicalGroupLimited*` as a folder exclusion * Use named volumes for dependency folders (the default since 1.12). To cancel a long build, press Ctrl + C once to stop gracefully, or twice to kill it. - - - ## Error codes | Code | Message | What it means | What to do | |------|---------|---------------|------------| | `TES-1001` | `virtualization not available` | Your CPU or OS doesn't expose hardware virtualization to Tessera. On Windows that usually means "Virtual Machine Platform" is disabled; on Linux, that your user can't access `/dev/kvm`. | Windows: `wsl --install --no-distribution`, then reboot. Linux: `sudo usermod -aG kvm $USER` and log in again. | | `TES-1007` | `VM disk is corrupted` | The disk image failed its checksum on startup, typically after a hard power-off or a full disk. | `tessera reset --keep-volumes`. If that fails, read the caution box at the top before reaching for `--hard`. | | `TES-2003` | `port 3000 already allocated` | Another process or workspace is bound to the host port. | See [Port 3000 is already in use](#port-3000-is-already-in-use-but-nothing-is-running). | | `TES-3010` | `image pull failed: unauthorized` | The registry rejected the credentials — an expired token, or your SSO session timed out. | `tessera registry login ghcr.io` (or your registry) and retry. | | `TES-4040` | `workspace not found` | You're not in a directory containing `tessera.yaml` and didn't pass `--workspace`. | `cd` into the project, or run `tessera up -w `. | | `TES-9999` | `internal error` | A bug. Sorry! | Collect a debug bundle (below) and [open an issue](https://github.com/acme/tessera/issues/new?template=bug_report.yml&labels=bug,triage&title=%5BTES-9999%5D+). | ### How do I collect a debug bundle for a bug report? 1. Reproduce the problem. 2. Run `tessera debug bundle`. It writes `tessera-debug-.tar.gz` to the current directory. 3. Attach it to your issue, or e-mail it to if it might contain anything sensitive.
What's inside the bundle? - `tessera.yaml`, with the values of keys matching `*token*`, `*secret*` and `*password*` replaced by `REDACTED` - the VM boot log and the last 10 000 lines of the daemon log - the output of `tessera doctor --json` - versions of Tessera, the host OS and the VM kernel Nothing is uploaded automatically.
